39676:
Judges is the second book of the *Nevi'im Rishonim* (Former Prophets), and Jewish tradition reads it as prophetic teaching rather than simple chronicle. Several haftarot come from it: the Song of Deborah (Judg 4:4-5:31) is read on Shabbat Shirah alongside the Song of the Sea, pairing Miriam's song with Deborah's; the birth of Samson (Judg 13) accompanies the Torah reading on the Nazirite (Num 4:21-7:89); and Jephthah's story (Judg 11:1-33) is read with the story of Israel's dealings with Sihon in Num 21. The rabbis loved Deborah as a prophetess and judge, though some also commented on her calling herself 'a mother in Israel' (Judg 5:7) as a sign of strong leadership.

The rabbis were troubled by Jephthah. A midrash (Genesis Rabbah 60:3; Leviticus Rabbah 37:4) says his vow was invalid and that the high priest Phinehas could have released him, but both were too proud to go to the other; so a daughter died through two men's pride. The verdict is that the Torah never wanted this. Gideon's refusal of kingship (Judg 8:23) became a classic text for the idea that God alone is Israel's king.

The first audience, living under kings, would have heard Judges as a mirror. The problem was not simply that there was no king; it was that Israel 'forgat the LORD their God' (Judg 3:7) and that each person did what was right in their own eyes. Yet even in this dark book God keeps hearing his people's cry. When Israel finally repents and puts away its gods, 'his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel' (Judg 10:16). The covenant relationship holds, not because Israel deserves it, but because God refuses to let his people go.
39678: Tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites and settle down beside them. A new generation arises that does not know the LORD.
39680: The narrator lays out the pattern of apostasy, oppression, crying out and deliverance that the book will follow.
39682: Othniel is a model deliverer; Ehud assassinates the Moabite king; Deborah, Barak and Jael defeat Sisera's chariots.

39685: An outcast becomes leader against Ammon, but his rash vow costs his daughter's life, and he fights a civil war with Ephraim.
39687: A Nazirite from birth, Samson follows his eyes, breaks his vows and is captured, yet in death he brings down the temple of Dagon.
39689: Private idols, a stolen priesthood, the atrocity at Gibeah and near-genocide of Benjamin show total collapse.

39751:
Ruth is set in the same dark period as Judges, but it reads like a different world. Instead of war and idolatry, we see a farming town, harvest fields, a threshing floor and a town gate where elders meet. A famine drives Elimelech, his wife Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem (which means 'house of bread') to Moab. The sons marry Moabite women. Then all three men die, leaving three widows with no sons.

In that world a widow without sons was in danger. Land and inheritance passed through men; a woman's security depended on husband, sons or male relatives. Israel's law tried to protect such people. Farmers had to leave the edges of their fields and the dropped stalks for 'the poor and the stranger' to glean (Lev 19:9-10; Deut 24:19). A close relative, the *go'el* (redeemer), was responsible for buying back family land sold in poverty (Lev 25:25) and for protecting family members. In the levirate custom, a dead man's brother married his widow to give him an heir (Deut 25:5-10). Ruth weaves these customs together, though the exact legal arrangements in Ruth 4 are debated, since Boaz is not a brother.

Ruth is a Moabite, and that matters. Moab was Israel's neighbour and rival, born, according to Genesis, from Lot's incest with his daughter (Gen 19:30-38). Deuteronomy says no Moabite shall enter the assembly of the LORD 'even to their tenth generation' (Deut 23:3), because Moab refused Israel bread and hired Balaam to curse them. Yet this Moabite woman shows more covenant loyalty than anyone in Judges. Later rabbis resolved the tension by reading the law as applying to Moabite men only (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3).

The book is a masterpiece of storytelling, built in four scenes: emptiness in Moab, a meeting in the field, a night at the threshing floor, and a legal settlement at the gate. Names carry meaning: Naomi ('pleasant') asks to be called Mara ('bitter') (Ruth 1:20); her sons Mahlon and Chilion sound like 'sickness' and 'wasting'; the nearer kinsman is left nameless, called in Hebrew 'so-and-so' (Ruth 4:1), because he refuses to preserve a name.
39753: The poor, widows and foreigners had a legal right to gather what reapers missed. Boaz goes beyond the law, telling his workers to drop extra stalks for Ruth.
39755: A close relative with the duty to buy back family land, free relatives from debt-slavery and protect the family name.
39757: A brother marries his dead brother's widow to raise an heir in the dead man's name. Ruth combines this idea with redemption of land.
39759: An open, flat area where grain was separated at harvest. Men often slept there to guard the grain. It could have associations with festivity and sexual license (compare Hos 9:1), which gives the night scene its tension.
39761: Ruth asks Boaz to 'spread thy skirt over thine handmaid', literally 'spread your wing', a request for marriage and protection (compare Ezek 16:8). It echoes Boaz's own blessing on her, taking refuge under God's wings.
39763: Handing over a sandal sealed a transfer of property rights; the narrator explains it as an old custom.
39764:
Ruth is one of the five *Megillot* (scrolls) read on festivals, and it is read on Shavuot, the feast of weeks, which celebrates both the wheat harvest and the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Tradition gives several reasons: the story takes place at harvest time (Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:23); Ruth's choice to join Israel ('thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God', Ruth 1:16) mirrors Israel accepting the Torah at Sinai; and by tradition David, Ruth's descendant, was born and died on Shavuot. Ruth is the model convert in Jewish law, and her words to Naomi shape the classic conversion process: the rabbis read each phrase as acceptance of a part of Jewish life (Yevamot 47b).

The midrash Ruth Rabbah observes that the scroll contains no laws of purity or impurity, of permitted or forbidden, and asks why it was written; its answer is: to teach how great is the reward of those who do acts of loving-kindness (*gemilut hasadim*). The key Hebrew word *hesed* (loyal, covenant love) appears three times (Ruth 1:8; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 3:10) and drives the whole book. Naomi blesses her daughters-in-law for their hesed; Boaz praises Ruth's hesed; and God's own hesed works quietly through their kindness. God acts directly only twice in the narrator's voice: giving bread (Ruth 1:6) and giving conception (Ruth 4:13).

For a first audience the point would be clear: covenant faithfulness is not only about bloodline. A foreign widow who binds herself to Israel's God, people and land by loyal love can become part of the family, and even the mother of kings. In the Hebrew Bible Ruth often follows Proverbs in the Writings, so that Ruth, whom Boaz calls 'a virtuous woman' (*eshet chayil*, Ruth 3:11), appears right after the poem of the 'virtuous woman' (Prov 31:10). She is that ideal in action.
39766: Naomi's family flees famine to Moab. Her husband and both sons die, leaving three widows.

The phrase 'spread thy skirt' recalls the image of God as Israel's husband (Ezek 16:8) and of the church as Christ's bride.
